Turf around St. Cloud pool cages and screened lanais

Turf around a St. Cloud pool or inside a screened lanai prices the same as a residential lawn, $8–$18 a square foot as of September 2026. St. Cloud's housing stock is young by Florida standards, with a median construction year in the 2000s, which means most pool cages in this town were built in an era when screen enclosures over a slab were already the norm.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Why sod fails first at the pool deck's edge

St. Cloud's housing is comparatively new, with a median year built in the 2000s, and a large share of that housing includes a screened pool cage poured on compacted fill right up to the deck edge. Sod struggles in that narrow strip worse than anywhere else on the lot: the fill drains differently than native soil, foot traffic concentrates right at the gate, and pool chemical splash browns a strip of grass that never gets a chance to recover between waterings. That combination is why the ring around a screened pool is one of the first places a St. Cloud homeowner asks about turf.

Lakefront lanais and the 10-foot setback

A smaller number of St. Cloud pool homes sit directly on East Lake Tohopekaliga or its connecting canal, with a screened lanai opening almost to the water. On a lot like that, turf around the pool cage still has to respect the state's 10-foot waterbody setback measured from the shoreline, not from the pool itself, unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the yard from the lake. A lanai built close to an unprotected bank has less usable turf area than the deck's footprint alone would suggest.

Grading a deck border toward the drain it already has

Most yards only need their base graded one to two percent away from the house, but a pool-deck border in St. Cloud gets aimed at the deck's existing low point instead, since runoff already sheds off the cage and coping onto that strip during every storm. Washed, open-graded crushed rock underneath keeps that added flow moving rather than binding into a crust at the transition where concrete meets soil. Skipping this and grading only away from the foundation leaves water pooling along the coping edge, which is exactly where bare feet cross most often on the way in and out of a St. Cloud cage.

Confirming the drain point before infill goes down

Once the drainage underlay is glued to a St. Cloud lanai floor but before any infill goes in, the crew runs water across the surface to confirm it actually reaches the deck's existing drain rather than pooling in a low spot the underlay created by accident. Catching a flat or misdirected section at this stage means lifting a corner of underlay and reworking it, which is straightforward before infill is down and considerably more disruptive after. This check takes a few minutes and is the reason a finished lanai floor rarely surprises anyone with standing water months later.

Say you have a 350 sq ft pool deck ring

Say you have a 350 sq ft ring of turf between a screened pool cage and the property's rear fence on a 2006 St. Cloud pool home, with the original sod worn to dirt along the gate path. At $10–$16 a square foot, that section runs roughly $3,850 to $5,600, glued and seamed to the concrete deck's edge with a drainage underlay so water clears the screen track instead of pooling against it. If the lot backs onto a canal, the layout also needs to confirm the 10-foot setback before the crew finalizes where the turf can start.

What does a small deck border cost, worked out?

Installed turf runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, typically ten to sixteen, and price does not change by St. Cloud ZIP code, only by access, base condition, and drainage. Say a homeowner wants a 250 sq ft strip between the pool cage and a side fence turfed rather than reseeded: at the typical range, that job runs somewhere between roughly twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars, before accounting for anything unusual about the site. A quote well outside that range for a plain open border, high or low, is worth asking about specifically, since the underlying material and labor do not vary by neighborhood.

Irrigation zones that used to wrap the pool cage

Older sprinkler layouts commonly ran a zone around the perimeter of a pool cage to keep sod alive right up to the screen, and that zone gets capped at the valve box the same as any other irrigation line once turf goes in, since the state's rule bars watering synthetic turf through an in-ground system entirely. Homeowners on Toho Water Authority's system, which absorbed St. Cloud's utility in October 2022, sometimes notice that capped zone show up as a small drop on the next bill rather than any change at all.

Why a slab that never fully dries is a warning sign

A glued lanai floor built without enough drainage underlay traps splash and rinse water against the concrete instead of routing it to the deck drain, and the first sign is usually a slab that stays damp longer after use than it should, not a visible puddle anyone notices right away in St. Cloud's humidity. Adhesive bonds weaker against a slab that never fully dries between uses, so a corner that lifts months after installation often traces back to that trapped moisture rather than a bad glue job on its own. Fixing it after the fact means pulling turf, not just adding infill.

Two reasons to rinse a pool border more than once a week in summer

Hosing down turf along a St. Cloud pool deck does two jobs at once: it clears chlorine or salt splash and pollen before either dries into the fibers, and it drops surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees ahead of an afternoon swim. Rainy-season storms between June and September handle some of that rinsing on their own, but the dry stretches on either side of summer leave splash as the only source of moisture on the turf, so a hose rinse earns its place in the routine year-round rather than just during the hottest weeks. Keeping shock and acid containers off the turf's edge avoids undoing the rinse entirely.

Questions people ask

Does turf around a St. Cloud pool cost more than a plain lawn?

It prices in the same range as a residential lawn, though small, glue-down sections against a concrete deck often land toward the upper half of that range because of the extra edge work and drainage underlay a slab requires.

Can I put turf right up to my lanai screen on a lake lot?

Only if the screen and pool sit outside the state's 10-foot waterbody setback, or if a seawall already separates the yard from the water. A site visit confirms the distance before any layout gets finalized.

What happens to my pool cage's old sprinkler zone?

It gets capped at the valve box during installation, since in-ground irrigation can't be used on synthetic turf under state rule. The rest of the system serving other parts of the yard keeps running normally.
